theory_query: Build a theory of how applying a day-of-year-windowed weighted local linear regression with WIDE smoothing windows (half-window h = 45 days, i.e. +/- 45 days of pooling) to reconstruct daily dew-point temperature from daily minimum temperature produces extreme over-prediction errors (dew points above 35 C) that are confined almost entirely to a SINGLE calendar month (November), with essentially zero errors in adjacent months (October 0.027%, November 1.556%, December 0.018%, and only 50 exceedances in total across January to July), in the north-eastern Amazon lowlands of Peru. The puzzle is the sharpness: a smoothing window spanning +/- 45 days should smear any smoothly varying seasonal effect across October to December, so how can the failure be confined to one month? Consider in particular whether an ABRUPT physical transition - the onset of the Amazonian wet season, which occurs around October-November - can produce a sharp single-month failure in a model whose smoothing window is deliberately broad, because the underlying transition is discontinuous while the fitted model is smooth. Also consider alternative mechanisms that could concentrate error into one month: regime switching or bimodal humidity distributions at onset, discontinuous land-atmosphere coupling and evapotranspiration recycling at wet-season onset, rapid changes in cloud cover and nocturnal cooling that decouple minimum temperature from moisture, and statistical artefacts such as day-of-year boundary effects, leverage of extreme training anomalies, or heteroscedastic residuals concentrated at the transition.
mission_statement: Scope: statistical reconstruction of gridded daily humidity from temperature in the humid tropics, focused on Amazonia. Prioritise evidence on: (1) the abruptness and timing of Amazonian wet-season onset and dry-to-wet transition, and whether near-surface humidity changes step-like or smoothly at onset; (2) predictability and model error during transition seasons versus established wet or dry seasons; (3) behaviour of kernel or local regression estimators near regime boundaries and discontinuities, including bias at breakpoints and the effect of bandwidth on boundary bias; (4) bimodality or regime switching in tropical near-surface humidity; (5) land-atmosphere coupling, moisture recycling and cloud-cover changes at wet-season onset that could decouple minimum temperature from dew point. Output should explain how a broad-bandwidth smooth model can fail sharply at an abrupt transition.
